answer.evidence: Three stepped wall blocks. Each has a stone top band (rows 0-8, 14-22, 28-37) that ends in a light front-edge line (rows 9, 23, 38) at L=189. A 1-row dark eave shadow follows (rows 10, 24, 39), then a darker south face of 4-7 rows (rows 10-13, 24-27, 39-45). The largest block, the south one, has a 10-row top and a 7-row front face. The dark columns at the left and right edges look like ground or shadow, not an isometric side face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small prop, so I judged it mostly on the measured facts. It has 14 visible tones per 16x16 tile against 12 and 10 for the references. Its near-flat coverage is 0%, the same as both references, so there are no large flat fills. Only 6% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, in line with the references at 7% and 9%, so the outline leans toward the adjacent material tone (grey-brown beside concrete, dark green beside weeds) and is not a black sticker line. By eye, each stepped block has a lighter top face and a darker south face. Cracks, speckle, green weeds and a warm rebar accent add variation. It has about 5 lightness steps on the concrete, slightly fewer than the roughly 6 on the references' roof and stone ramps. That is acceptable for a small ruin piece. Its raw palette is only 20 colours, but the visible tone count matches the references, so it would sit acceptably beside them.
